title: Bières de la Meuse [Beers from the Meuse River]
credit: Gift of Harry A. Starr · On loan from the Herbert F. Johnson Museum of Art, Cornell University
description: The figure, draped cloth, and surrounding ornament share a flowing rhythm. Seen beside the gathered garments, the lithograph invites comparison between folds drawn on paper and folds built in fabric. Both can direct attention through a figure, although one fixes its lines in an image and the other changes with the body.
alt: Bières de la Meuse [Beers from the Meuse River]
assetNote: Detail shown from the supplied installation mockup; a separate artwork photograph has not yet been located.

title: La Dame aux Camélias—Sarah Bernhardt
credit: Gift of Harry A. Starr · On loan from the Herbert F. Johnson Museum of Art, Cornell University
description: An elongated figure occupies a narrow decorative frame. The format encourages the eye to travel vertically through the represented clothing, linking the proportions of the image with those of the dressed body. Compare that visual length with the gathered garments beside it.
assetNote: Detail shown from the supplied installation mockup; a separate artwork photograph has not yet been located.

title: La Samaritaine
credit: Acquired through the Membership Purchase Fund · On loan from the Herbert F. Johnson Museum of Art, Cornell University
description: The tall format places a dressed figure within an architectural arrangement of lettering and ornament. Follow the relationship between the figure’s silhouette and its surrounding frame. The poster offers a different way to construct proportion from the gathered cloth displayed nearby.
assetNote: Detail shown from the supplied installation mockup; a separate artwork photograph has not yet been located.

title: Untitled [Figure in ancient Greek dress]
credit: Gift of Frank P. DiPrima · On loan from the Herbert F. Johnson Museum of Art, Cornell University
description: This painted figure in ancient Greek dress presents cloth through the artist’s arrangement of line, color, and light. Compare the suggested fall of its fabric with the actual garments in the case. What can a painted fold communicate, and what remains a matter of imagination?
assetNote: Detail shown from the supplied installation mockup; a separate artwork photograph has not yet been located.

title: Job
credit: Gift of Isabel and William Berley, Classes of 1947 and 1945 · On loan from the Herbert F. Johnson Museum of Art, Cornell University
description: Curving lines surround the figure and draw attention between body and ornament. Beside the garments, the lithograph encourages us to consider how a visual rhythm can extend beyond clothing into the composition around it.
assetNote: Detail shown from the supplied installation mockup; a separate artwork photograph has not yet been located.

title: The Fabric Guide: Textile Sample Book
credit: On loan from the Kheel Center for Labor-Management Documentation and Archives, Cornell University Library
footer: On loan from the Kheel Center for Labor-Management Documentation and Archives, Cornell University Library
description: A sample book brings textile surfaces into a format intended for close comparison. Its pages connect the appearance of cloth with material examples, offering a historical counterpart to the contemporary tactile pages made for this exhibition. The original book remains in the case; the newly made samples are the ones visitors may handle.
alt: The Fabric Guide: Textile Sample Book

title: Seated Figure Restored as the Muse Urania
material: Plaster cast after a Roman marble sculpture of the late first century CE, based on a Hellenistic Greek model
credit: On loan from the Cornell Cast Collection
description: Cloth folds gather around the seated figure and change direction across its bent legs. The cast translates a draped body into a fixed surface, while the garments nearby remain flexible textiles. Compare how each makes the body visible through the layers surrounding it.
alt: Seated Figure Restored as the Muse Urania

title: Standing Woman with Hat and Fan
material: Painted terracotta replica in Hellenistic Greek style
credit: On loan from the Cornell Cast Collection
description: The figure’s mantle encloses much of the body, while its folds suggest the pose beneath. The painted terracotta replica invites comparison with garments whose outer layers create an outline of their own. Its nineteenth-century manufacture is distinct from the Hellenistic style it recalls.
alt: Standing Woman with Hat and Fan

title: Standing Woman with Mirror
material: Painted terracotta replica after a figure probably dating to the third or second century BCE
credit: On loan from the Cornell Cast Collection
description: The draped figure offers another arrangement of cloth around a standing body. Follow where folds draw inward and where they hang away. As a later painted terracotta replica, the object also makes visible how ancient forms circulated through reproduction.

title: Seated Woman with Writing Tablet
material: Painted terracotta replica in Hellenistic Greek style
credit: On loan from the Cornell Cast Collection
description: A seated pose changes the surfaces over which cloth falls. This painted terracotta replica provides a point of comparison for the standing figures and hanging garments in Layers: posture and enclosure work together to shape the visible folds.
assetNote: Image from the Cornell Cast Collection record supplied with the exhibition files.

title: Aphrodite Fréjus (Louvre–Naples Type)
material: Plaster cast after a Roman marble sculpture, circa 75–125 CE, based on a Greek original of circa 420–400 BCE
credit: On loan from the Cornell Cast Collection
description: The figure’s stance and the direction of its drapery provide a sculptural comparison for Posture. Look between shoulders, hips, and the cloth crossing the body. This late nineteenth-century cast reproduces a Roman sculpture based on an earlier Greek original, carrying the pose through successive acts of interpretation.

title: Pair of Ceramic Vessels in Black-Figure Style
credit: Courtesy of the Cornell Anthropology Collections, uncatalogued
footer: Courtesy of the Cornell Anthropology Collections, uncatalogued
description: Dark figures and decorative bands organize the curved surfaces of these vessels. Compare their borders with the decorated edges of nearby garments: an edge can frame a scene, interrupt a surface, or direct the eye around an object. The supplied record does not establish an ancient date for these vessels.
alt: Pair of Ceramic Vessels in Black-Figure Style
assetNote: Photograph shows one of the pair of vessels.

title: Decorative Plate with Greek-Key Border and Mythological Figure
credit: Courtesy of the Cornell Anthropology Collections
description: The Greek-key border circles a central mythological figure, separating the image from the plate’s edge. Its repeated turns create a visual rhythm around a concentrated center. Compare this arrangement with a garment whose ornament frames a neckline or hem.
alt: Decorative Plate with Greek-Key Border and Mythological Figure

title: Framed Egyptian-Style Papyrus Painting with Offering Scene
credit: Courtesy of the Cornell Anthropology Collections
description: Figures and signs are arranged across the painted papyrus as an offering scene. In this case, the image provides a point of comparison for the garments’ use of color and ornament. Its Egyptian-style imagery should be distinguished from a confirmed ancient date, which the supplied record does not provide.
alt: Framed Egyptian-Style Papyrus Painting with Offering Scene

title: Egyptian-Style Relief Tile with Standing Figures and Hieroglyphs
credit: Courtesy of the Cornell Anthropology Collections
description: Standing figures and hieroglyphic forms occupy a narrow painted relief surface. Color and raised detail offer different ways to emphasize the scene. Compare those effects with the garments’ combination of colored borders and reflective embellishment.
alt: Egyptian-Style Relief Tile with Standing Figures and Hieroglyphs

title: Egyptian Revival Decorative Vase with Figural Scene
credit: Courtesy of the Cornell Anthropology Collections, uncatalogued
footer: Courtesy of the Cornell Anthropology Collections, uncatalogued
description: Figural decoration follows the vase’s curved surface, combining imagery with bands of contrasting color. The object’s Egyptian Revival designation describes a later reimagining of Egyptian forms. It encourages comparison with fashion’s own selective use of motifs associated with antiquity.
alt: Egyptian Revival Decorative Vase with Figural Scene

title: Egyptian-Style Beaded Necklace
credit: Courtesy of the Cornell Anthropology Collections
description: Rows of colored plastic beads form a broad, repeated pattern around an opening for the neck. The necklace demonstrates how color and arrangement can evoke an ornamental language without relying on precious materials. Compare its visual effect with the metal strips and metallic threads in the garments.
